item.text:
1. **Section 2(1)(A) — 10,000-ton threshold.** The prohibition permits recovery of up to 10,000 metric tons annually, even if that activity causes serious ecological harm or is plainly commercial.

2. **Section 2(1)(A) — Vessel-by-vessel calculation.** Because the threshold applies “by a single vessel,” a company could divide one mining operation among multiple vessels, affiliates, or contractors and keep each vessel below the limit.

3. **Section 2(1)(A) — Undefined annual period.** “Per year” does not specify a calendar year, fiscal year, license year, or rolling 12-month period, inviting manipulation and disputes about when recovered tonnage counts.

4. **Section 2(1)(A) — Enforcement only after the threshold is crossed.** Whether an operation constitutes prohibited mining may not be knowable until it recovers its 10,001st ton; the bill does not authorize injunctions based on planned or imminent recovery above the threshold.

5. **Section 2(1)(A) — “Recovery” is undefined.** Operators could argue that collection, lifting, dredging, stockpiling, initial processing, or recovery by remotely operated equipment is not “recovery” by the vessel.

6. **Section 2(1)(A) — Depth measurement is unclear.** The bill does not say whether “depths greater than 200 meters” means water depth, distance below the seabed, or another measurement, or how depth is determined across a variable mining site.

7. **Section 2(1)(A) — Shallow seabed loophole.** Industrial seabed mining at 200 meters or less is categorically outside the definition, regardless of its scale or environmental effects.

8. **Section 2(1)(A) — “Mineral resources” is undefined.** Companies could litigate whether particular deposits, ores, crusts, sediments, dissolved materials, or materials recovered alongside minerals qualify.

9. **Section 2(1)(B) — “Secretary” is not identified.** The Act never defines which Cabinet secretary makes comparable-risk determinations, creating uncertainty over whether the authority belongs to Commerce, Interior, State, or another department.

10. **Section 2(1)(B) — Unspecified determination process.** There is no procedure, deadline, evidentiary standard, rulemaking authority, or judicial-review framework for determining that another activity poses comparable risks. Until an affirmative determination is completed, the activity may remain outside the prohibition.

11. **Section 2(1)(B) — Unclear comparator.** “Risks…comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A)” does not identify which activity, ecosystem, scale, or type of risk supplies the benchmark and may be challenged as impermissibly vague.

12. **Section 2(2) — Incomplete definition of “U.S. person.”** The definition omits U.S. nationals, permanent residents, partnerships, LLCs and other unincorporated entities, trusts, associations, and potentially federally or territorially incorporated entities.

13. **Section 2(2) — Foreign-subsidiary loophole.** A U.S. company could conduct mining through a separately incorporated foreign subsidiary or joint venture because the bill contains no ownership-or-control test or anti-evasion rule.

14. **Sections 2 and 3 — “Person” is not expressly defined.** Although the Dictionary Act may supply a default definition, an express definition is important here to ensure that partnerships, associations, government entities, vessel owners, operators, contractors, and other legal persons are covered.

15. **Section 2(3) — Covered-vessel tonnage threshold.** Vessels of exactly 5,000 gross tons or less escape registration, even if they conduct substantial mining or operate together as a fleet.

16. **Section 2(3) — “Gross tons” is ambiguous.** The bill does not specify the applicable tonnage convention or measurement system, allowing disputes over whether a vessel exceeds 5,000 gross tons.

17. **Section 2(3) — “Equipped for” is easy to evade.** Modular equipment could be installed after registration would otherwise be required, placed on support vessels, or characterized as exploration or research equipment.

18. **Section 3(a) — “Engage in” is undefined.** It is unclear whether the prohibition covers financing, sponsoring, directing, controlling, contracting for, insuring, transporting, processing, purchasing, or otherwise facilitating mining, rather than only physically extracting minerals.

19. **Section 3(a) — Geographic coverage is uncertain.** “In the United States” does not expressly include U.S. territorial waters, the exclusive economic zone, the outer continental shelf, U.S.-flagged vessels, or U.S. facilities abroad.

20. **Section 3(a) — Foreign operators on U.S. vessels may escape.** A foreign person operating through a U.S.-flagged vessel outside the United States is not necessarily a “U.S. person,” and the bill does not independently prohibit covered conduct by U.S.-flagged vessels.

21. **Section 3(a) — No prohibition on permits or preparations.** The provision bans only engaging in the defined mining, not issuing licenses, prospecting, testing equipment, building mining systems, entering extraction contracts, or otherwise preparing to mine.

22. **Section 3(b) — Exception swallows the rule for exploration licensees.** It exempts “mining” conducted under a pre-enactment exploration license, even though an exploration license ordinarily should not authorize commercial extraction.

23. **Section 3(b) — License issuer is unspecified.** The exception could encompass a license issued by any foreign government, international body, or other entity, including one with weak standards or no legitimate jurisdiction.

24. **Section 3(b) — No validity or good-standing requirement.** A revoked, expired, dormant, fraudulently obtained, or legally defective exploration license could be asserted as the basis for the exemption.

25. **Section 3(b) — No limits on grandfathered operations.** The exception has no expiration date and does not restrict transfer, assignment, renewal, amendment, expansion, production volume, mining method, or geographic area.

26. **Section 3(c) — Environmental-assessment exemption is unlimited.** Any operator could claim that extraction is for environmental assessment because the bill imposes no volume cap, independent approval, scientific protocol, noncommercial-purpose requirement, or prohibition on selling recovered minerals.

27. **Section 3(c) — Mixed-purpose operations are unaddressed.** “For the purpose of” does not say whether environmental assessment must be the sole, primary, or merely one incidental purpose, allowing commercial mining to be packaged with research.

28. **Section 4(a) — “Operator” is undefined.** Ownership, management, chartering, remote control, and subcontracting arrangements could make it unclear who must register and could leave multiple parties disclaiming responsibility.

29. **Section 4(a) — No registration mechanics.** The bill supplies no deadline, required information, updating obligation, implementing authority, or rule for vessels that become covered after operations begin.

30. **Section 4(a) — Overbroad yet incomplete jurisdiction.** “Each covered vessel” could be read to require registration by foreign vessels with no U.S. nexus, which would be difficult to defend or enforce, while smaller vessels and non-vessel mining platforms are omitted.

31. **Section 4(b) — Reporting requirement is vague.** The bill does not prescribe filing dates, report contents, tonnage calculations, location data, records retention, supporting documentation, audit rights, or a duty to correct inaccurate reports.

32. **Section 4(b) — Self-certification is weak.** Reports are certified only by the operator, with no required responsible officer, independent verification, monitoring equipment, or explicit penalty for false or incomplete certification.

33. **Sections 4 and 5 — Registration and reporting are unenforceable.** Section 5 penalizes only violations of section 3, so failure to register or report is not itself subject to the Act’s civil or criminal penalties.

34. **Section 4 — No transparency provision.** Reports need not be made public, transmitted to Congress, or shared with enforcement agencies, limiting outside scrutiny and the bill’s public-education value.

35. **Section 5 — No designated enforcing authority or process.** The bill does not identify the agency that investigates violations, assesses civil penalties, issues subpoenas, conducts hearings, or refers cases to the Department of Justice.

36. **Section 5 — Essential enforcement remedies are missing.** There is no express authority for injunctions, vessel detention, forfeiture, mineral seizure, disgorgement, restoration orders, permit revocation, or recovery of response and environmental-remediation costs.

37. **Section 5(a) — Daily-violation calculation is unclear.** The bill does not explain when a violation begins or ends, particularly where the 10,000-ton annual threshold is crossed late in the year or extraction occurs intermittently.

38. **Section 5(a) — Penalty may be merely optional.** “Not more than” $1,000,000 sets no minimum penalty and supplies no mandatory assessment factors, potentially allowing nominal penalties that mining companies treat as a cost of doing business.

39. **Section 5(b) — “Willfully” creates a high criminal burden.** Prosecutors may have to prove knowledge that the conduct was unlawful, not merely intentional mining, and the bill contains no alternative knowing or reckless offense.

40. **Section 5 — No express secondary liability.** The Act does not clearly cover attempts, conspiracy, aiding and abetting, causing a violation, concealment, or evasion through affiliates and contractors.

41. **Sections 5(a) and 8 — Conflicting timing language.** Section 5(a) refers to violations occurring on or after enactment, but the entire Act—including section 3—does not take effect for 180 days, creating needless uncertainty about when liability begins.

42. **Section 6 — Weak international mandate.** Requiring the Secretary of State merely to “seek to negotiate” does not require negotiations to begin, benchmarks to be met, an agreement to be concluded, or progress to be reported to Congress.

43. **Section 6 — “Equivalent” reproduces the bill’s loopholes.** An agreement need only establish prohibitions equivalent to section 3, including its tonnage threshold, license exception, and environmental-assessment exception, rather than a comprehensive ban.

44. **Section 7(a) — National Academies report is not required.** The provision does not direct any agency to commission the report, fund it, set its scope, or establish scientific criteria, leaving “acting on a report” uncertain.

45. **Section 7(a) — Termination standard is undefined.** “Serious harm” has no definition, baseline, burden of proof, precautionary standard, or treatment of cumulative, irreversible, and poorly understood effects.

46. **Section 7(a) — Joint-resolution procedure is incomplete.** The bill does not specify the required resolution text, referral, expedited procedures, or whether the finding must address particular mining technologies, locations, and impacts.

47. **Section 7 — Internal duration conflict.** Subsection (a) says the prohibition remains until Congress makes a safety finding, while subsection (b) terminates the entire Act after 10 years regardless of whether Congress ever makes that finding.

48. **Section 7(b) — Automatic sunset defeats a durable prohibition.** Mining becomes lawful automatically after 10 years without any scientific finding, replacement safeguards, or affirmative congressional vote; registration, reporting, penalties, and the international mandate also disappear.

49. **Section 8 — 180-day delay permits a mining rush.** Companies can commence or accelerate operations before the Act becomes effective, and the bill contains no interim restriction, preservation order, or treatment of minerals recovered during the delay.

50. **Act-wide — No coordination with existing seabed-mining law.** The bill does not amend or suspend existing licensing authorities, prohibit issuance or renewal of licenses, or explain its relationship to existing permits and statutes, creating conflicting legal commands and avoidable litigation.

51. **Act-wide — No implementing-rule authority or deadline.** The legislation depends on unresolved technical questions but does not clearly authorize an agency to issue regulations, establish measurement methods, require monitoring, or close evasive practices.

52. **Act-wide — No monitoring or inspection authority.** Agencies receive no express power to inspect vessels and records, require tracking or sampling equipment, obtain operational data, or verify where and how much material was recovered.
